---
title: "Single-cell pseudobulk analysis: worked solutions"
format: html
---

# Setup

Run the chunks in order. This notebook uses a course RDS file; update the path
below if your data are elsewhere. The analysis compares reporter-positive and
reporter-negative cells across three paired pools.

## Load packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(batchelor)
library(edgeR)
library(scater)
library(ggplot2)
library(scran)
library(pheatmap)
library(scuttle)
```

## Load data

The data were prepared as described in the
[Carpentries tutorial](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/bioc-scrnaseq/multi-sample.html#setup-and-data-exploration)
and saved as an RDS file. Rows are genes and columns are cells.

```{r}
sce <- readRDS("/storage/olin0164/single_cell/pseudobulk/sce.rds")
```

# First steps

Inspect the `SingleCellExperiment` object.

```{r}
sce
```

Inspect the cell metadata with `colData()`.

```{r}
colData(sce)
```

# Preprocess the data

## Prepare sample labels

Convert `sample` to a factor so that plots treat sample identifiers as categories.

```{r}
sce$sample <- as.factor(sce$sample)
```

## Quality filtering

Remove cells already labelled as stripped nuclei or doublets in the metadata.

```{r}
drop <- sce$celltype.mapped %in% c("stripped", "Doublet")

sce <- sce[, !drop]
```

## Bonus: subsample cells

To reduce computation, try retaining a random 50% of cells from each sample
after filtering. Set a seed and sample within each sample separately.
The main solution uses all retained cells. Subsampling adds variability to
cell type counts, so use the full data for the abundance analysis where possible.

## Normalisation

Use `logNormCounts()` to adjust for library size and log-transform the normalised
counts. Assign the updated object to `sce`.

```{r}
sce <- logNormCounts(sce)
sce
```

The updated object contains a `"logcounts"` assay; the original `"counts"` assay is retained.

## Model gene variance

Use `modelGeneVar()` to estimate total, technical, and biological variance per
gene. Set `block = sce$sample` to model variation within samples, then combine
the estimates. Store the result in `dec`.

```{r}
dec <- modelGeneVar(sce, block = sce$sample)
dec
```

The result contains one row per gene. `per.block` holds sample-specific results;
see `?scran::modelGeneVar` for details.

## Select highly variable genes

Select genes with positive estimated biological variance. Store the logical
selection in `chosen.hvgs` and count selected (`TRUE`) and unselected (`FALSE`) genes.

```{r}
chosen.hvgs <- dec$bio > 0
table(chosen.hvgs)
```

## Apply PCA

Use principal component analysis (PCA) to summarise variation across cells using
the selected genes. `subset_row` specifies the genes to use; when supplied,
`ntop` is ignored, so it is omitted here.

```{r}
set.seed(10102)
sce <- runPCA(sce, subset_row = chosen.hvgs)
sce
```

PCA coordinates are stored in `reducedDim(sce, "PCA")`.

## Apply t-SNE

Use t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) to create a
two-dimensional layout from the PCA coordinates. Assign the result to `sce`.

```{r}
set.seed(10102)
sce <- runTSNE(sce, dimred = "PCA")
sce
```

The layout is stored in `reducedDim(sce, "TSNE")`.

## Visualise the t-SNE layout

Plot the t-SNE coordinates with `ggplot2`, colouring cells by sample.

```{r}
tsne_plot_data <- cbind(
    reducedDim(sce, "TSNE"),
    colData(sce)
)
ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = TSNE1, y = TSNE2, colour = sample)) +
    labs(colour = "Sample") +
    geom_point(size = 0.2) +
    guides(
        colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))
    ) +
    theme_classic()
```

Colour the same layout by `celltype.mapped`. Move the legend below the plot
and reduce its size to fit the cell type labels. Quarto options `fig-height`
and `fig-width` control figure dimensions in inches.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
tsne_plot_data <- cbind(
    reducedDim(sce, "TSNE"),
    colData(sce)
)
ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = TSNE1, y = TSNE2, colour = celltype.mapped)) +
    labs(colour = "Cell type") +
    geom_point(size = 0.2) +
    guides(
        colour = guide_legend(
            position = "bottom",
            override.aes = list(size = 1)
        )
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(
        legend.key.size = grid::unit(0.3, "line"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7)
    )
```

## Correct batch effects

Sample separation may reflect technical effects, biological differences, or both.
Use batch correction to help compare cell types across samples, while checking
that meaningful biological differences remain.

Use `batchelor::correctExperiments()` with `FastMnnParam()`:

- Set a seed for randomised steps.
- Use `batch` to identify samples and `subset.row` to select genes.
- Set `merge.order` to merge samples within each reporter group before merging
  the groups. The indices refer to batch order; check this against your sample metadata.

Store the result in `merged`. Batch-corrected coordinates are for visualisation;
use original counts for differential expression.

```{r}
table(sce$sample, sce$tomato)
set.seed(10102)

merged <- correctExperiments(
    sce,
    batch = sce$sample,
    subset.row = chosen.hvgs,
    PARAM = FastMnnParam(
        merge.order = list(
            list(1, 3, 5), # Reporter-positive (3 pools)
            list(2, 4, 6)  # Reporter-negative (3 pools)
        )
    )
)
merged
```

The result includes a `"reconstructed"` assay and corrected coordinates in
`reducedDim(merged, "corrected")`. These are not raw counts.

## Apply t-SNE to the corrected data

Apply t-SNE to the corrected coordinates.

```{r}
set.seed(10102)
merged <- runTSNE(merged, dimred = "corrected")
merged
```

This replaces the `"TSNE"` layout in `merged`; the uncorrected layout remains in `sce`.

## Visualise t-SNE after correction

Plot the new `"TSNE"` layout, colouring cells by batch (sample).

```{r}
tsne_plot_data <- cbind(
    reducedDim(merged, "TSNE"),
    colData(merged)
)
ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = TSNE1, y = TSNE2, colour = batch)) +
    labs(colour = "Sample") +
    geom_point(size = 0.2) +
    guides(
        colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))
    ) +
    theme_classic()
```

Repeat the plot with cells coloured by cell type. Compare it with the uncorrected layout.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
tsne_plot_data <- cbind(
    reducedDim(merged, "TSNE"),
    colData(merged)
)
ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = TSNE1, y = TSNE2, colour = celltype.mapped)) +
    labs(colour = "Cell type") +
    geom_point(size = 0.2) +
    guides(
        colour = guide_legend(
            position = "bottom",
            override.aes = list(size = 1)
        )
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(
        legend.key.size = grid::unit(0.3, "line"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7)
    )
```

# Prepare for differential expression

## Aggregate cells into pseudobulks

Sum original counts for each cell type within each sample using
`scuttle::aggregateAcrossCells()`. Each column of the result is one cell-type/sample
combination. Biological replication comes from the samples, not individual cells.

Use the filtered, uncorrected `sce` so that all genes remain available for testing.

```{r}
summed <- aggregateAcrossCells(
    sce,
    ids = colData(sce)[, c("celltype.mapped", "sample")],
    use.assay.type = "counts"
)

summed
```

Inspect `ncol(summed)` to count pseudobulk profiles (192 in the original example).
These are cell-type/sample combinations, not 192 independent biological samples.

## Prepare the data for edgeR

Start with one cell type, `"Mesenchyme"`. Store its pseudobulk profiles in `current`.

```{r}
current <- summed[, summed$celltype.mapped == "Mesenchyme"]
current
```

Create a `DGEList`, the count-and-metadata container used by `edgeR`.

```{r}
y <- DGEList(counts(current), samples = colData(current))
y
```

## Check for samples with insufficient data

The `ncells` metadata column records the number of cells in each pseudobulk.
Remove profiles based on fewer than 10 cells. This example threshold reduces
unstable estimates; check that enough replicates remain in both conditions.

```{r}
discarded <- current$ncells < 10

y <- y[, !discarded]

table(discarded)
```

## Check for genes with insufficient data

Use `filterByExpr()` to exclude genes with insufficient expression. Supply the
condition labels from the filtered `y$samples` so they match the retained columns.

```{r}
keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = y$samples$tomato)

y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]

table(keep)
```

## Normalise

Use `calcNormFactors()` to estimate trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) scaling
factors. These adjust effective library sizes for differences in RNA composition;
they do not replace the counts.

```{r}
y <- calcNormFactors(y)

y$samples
```

Inspect `y$samples$norm.factors` to see the sample-specific scaling factors.

## Visualise the effect of normalisation

Use `plotMD()` to compare each sample with the others. The x-axis shows average
log-expression; the y-axis shows log-fold differences.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

for (i in seq_len(ncol(y))) {
    plotMD(y, column = i)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Check for broad centring around zero and sample-specific patterns. These plots
are diagnostics, not proof that normalisation has removed all unwanted variation.

Use multidimensional scaling (MDS) to explore sample similarities. Samples with
similar log-expression profiles should be closer together.

```{r}
limma::plotMDS(
    cpm(y, log = TRUE),
    col = ifelse(y$samples$tomato, "red", "blue"),
    labels = y$samples$sample
)
legend("topright", legend = c("Reporter-positive", "Reporter-negative"),
       col = c("red", "blue"), pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

Check whether samples group by condition or pool and look for outliers. The
orientation and separation of the plot can change with the data.

## Prepare the design matrix

Create a design matrix with `pool` to account for the paired design and `tomato`
to represent reporter status. The final coefficient compares `TRUE` (reporter-positive)
with `FALSE` (reporter-negative), adjusting for pool.

```{r}
design <- model.matrix(
    ~ factor(pool) + factor(tomato),
    data = y$samples
)
design
```

## Estimate dispersion

Use `estimateDisp()` to estimate negative binomial dispersion: variation between
replicate profiles beyond that expected from counting noise.

```{r}
y <- estimateDisp(y, design)

summary(y$trended.dispersion)
```

## Visualise the biological coefficient of variation

Use `plotBCV()` to show the biological coefficient of variation (BCV, the square
root of dispersion) against average log counts per million (CPM). The plot also
shows common and trended estimates.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 7
plotBCV(y)
```

## Fit a model for each gene

Fit a quasi-likelihood (QL) negative binomial generalised linear model for each
gene with `glmQLFit()`. `robust = TRUE` limits the influence of genes with unusual
variability when estimating the shared dispersion prior.

```{r}
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design, robust = TRUE)

names(fit)
```

## Visualise gene-wise quasi-dispersion

Use `plotQLDisp()` to inspect gene-wise quasi-likelihood dispersion estimates
against average log2 CPM.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 7
plotQLDisp(fit)
```

# Differential expression

## Perform the test

See the [edgeR reference manual](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/edgeR/man/edgeR.pdf)
for details of the modelling and testing functions.

Use `glmQLFTest()` to test the final design coefficient: reporter-positive versus
reporter-negative cells within this cell type, adjusting for pool. `decideTests()`
uses a 5% false discovery rate (FDR) by default.

```{r}
res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = ncol(design))

summary(decideTests(res))
```

## Access the results

Use `topTags()` to rank genes by p-value. The FDR column adjusts for testing
many genes; top-ranked genes are not necessarily statistically significant.

**Bonus:** Which argument changes the number of rows returned? (Answer: `n`.)

```{r}
topTags(res)
```

# Repeat differential expression for all cell types

Use `scran::pseudoBulkDGE()` to run the workflow separately for each cell type.
Retain profiles with at least 10 cells and use the same paired design.

```{r}
summed.filt <- summed[, summed$ncells >= 10]

de.results <- pseudoBulkDGE(
    summed.filt,
    label = summed.filt$celltype.mapped,
    design = ~ factor(pool) + tomato,
    coef = "tomatoTRUE",
    condition = summed.filt$tomato
)
```

Inspect the Mesenchyme results and compare them with the manual workflow.
Exact agreement depends on using the same filtering and model settings.

```{r}
cur.results <- de.results[["Mesenchyme"]]

cur.results[order(cur.results$PValue), ]
```

# Differential abundance

## Quantify cell type abundance per sample

Count cells of each type in each sample. Here, rows represent cell types and
columns represent samples; this analysis tests relative cell type abundance.

```{r}
abundances <- table(merged$celltype.mapped, merged$sample)
abundances
```

Use `unclass()` to remove the `table` class while keeping the count matrix.

```{r}
abundances <- unclass(abundances)
abundances
```

## Design matrix and dispersion

Use `match()` to retrieve one metadata row per sample, in abundance-matrix
column order. Only sample-level fields such as `pool` and `tomato` are used below;
cell-level annotations in these rows do not describe the whole sample.

```{r}
extra.info <- colData(merged)[match(colnames(abundances), merged$sample), ]
extra.info
```

Create a `DGEList` from cell type counts and sample metadata. Its library sizes
are the total retained cell counts per sample.

```{r}
y.ab <- DGEList(abundances, samples = extra.info)
y.ab
```

Create the paired design matrix with `pool` and reporter status (`tomato`).

```{r}
design <- model.matrix(~ factor(pool) + factor(tomato), y.ab$samples)
design
```

Estimate negative binomial dispersion with `robust = TRUE`.

```{r}
y.ab <- estimateDisp(y.ab, design, robust = TRUE)
y.ab
```

## Use total cell counts as library sizes

See the [Carpentries discussion of compositional effects](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/bioc-scrnaseq/multi-sample.html#background-on-compositional-effect).

Without TMM scaling, edgeR still adjusts for total retained cell counts through
its library sizes. This tests changes in cell type proportions, not absolute
cell numbers. An increase in one type can reduce the proportions of others.

Fit one QL model per cell type. Use `abundance.trend = FALSE` because cell types
need not follow the expression-dependent variability trend used for genes.

```{r}
fit.ab <- glmQLFit(y.ab, design, robust = TRUE, abundance.trend = FALSE)
fit.ab
```

Test the final coefficient, which compares reporter-positive with reporter-negative
samples while accounting for pool. Summarise calls at the default 5% FDR.

```{r}
res <- glmQLFTest(fit.ab, coef = ncol(design))
summary(decideTests(res))
```

Display the top 10 cell types ranked by p-value. Check FDR values: the table
can include non-significant results, and only a subset of significant types may
be shown.

```{r}
topTags(res, n = 10)
```

A negative `logFC` indicates lower relative abundance in reporter-positive
(`tomato = TRUE`) samples; a positive value indicates higher relative abundance.

## Apply TMM scaling

Use `calcNormFactors()` to add TMM scaling to the total-cell-count library sizes.
This uses the assumption that most cell types are unchanged, or that increases
and decreases are roughly balanced. It still measures relative abundance.

```{r}
y.ab2 <- calcNormFactors(y.ab)
y.ab2
```

Compare the normalisation factors before and after TMM scaling.

```{r}
cat("after calcNormFactors", fill = TRUE)
y.ab2$samples$norm.factors
cat("without calcNormFactors", fill = TRUE)
y.ab$samples$norm.factors
```

Refit dispersions and QL models, then repeat the test with TMM scaling.

```{r}
y.ab2 <- estimateDisp(y.ab2, design, robust = TRUE)
fit.ab2 <- glmQLFit(y.ab2, design, robust = TRUE, abundance.trend = FALSE)
res2 <- glmQLFTest(fit.ab2, coef = ncol(design))
```

Count significant results at the default 5% FDR.

```{r}
summary(decideTests(res2))
```

Display the ranked results.

```{r}
topTags(res2, n = 10)
```

Compare effect sizes and FDRs between the two approaches. Similar numbers of
significant results do not imply identical estimates.

## Test against a log-fold change threshold

Return to the model without TMM scaling and use `glmTreat()` to test whether
the absolute log2 fold change exceeds 1 (more than a two-fold change). This
tests a minimum effect size; it does not distinguish compositional changes
from changes in absolute cell numbers.

```{r}
res.lfc <- glmTreat(fit.ab, coef = ncol(design), lfc = 1)
```

Count cell types significant at the default 5% FDR.

```{r}
summary(decideTests(res.lfc))
```

Display cell types, log2 fold changes, p-values, and FDRs.

```{r}
topTags(res.lfc)
```
